messages.subject: program distance data setup for importing,
messages.subject_clean: program distance data setup for importing,
messages.body_plain:
I'd appreciate any help anyone can provide.  I'm pretty new to distance
sampling, and would like to use the program DISTANCE to calculate
population estimates of mottled ducks.  The survey has 8 transects and 2
point counts.  I have the lengths and areas of each.  The survey is
conducted every 2 weeks all year long.  For the past 2 years, we've been
collecting distance data on mottled ducks.

My question is hopefully simple- what's the best way to set up the data
for importing and analysis?

I've looked through the documentation, and couldn't really find how to
deal with time series.  Should I count every biweekly survey as a separate
estimate?

Peter Keller
Refuge Operations Specialist
US Fish & Wildlife Service
Aransas/Matagorda Island National Wildlife Refuge Complex
PO Box 100, Austwell, TX 77950
(361)286-3559 ext. 236, Fax (361)286-3722

messages.subject: Re: program distance data setup for importing,
messages.subject_clean: program distance data setup for importing,
messages.body_plain:
Peter-

I know zilch about mottled ducks, your eventual goals for the work and
how many detections you will get per survey and inter-transect
variability.  Each is essential
to answer your questions.  Also, you said you have 8 transects and 2
point counts.  Do you really mean that you have a
combined line transect and point transect survey?  If so, there is no
way to handle that in Distance.  Never run into a situation in which
both types were needed for a single analysis.  That will be a problem.
With regard to your question about time series.  There is no
specific way to handle time series in Distance.  If you want an estimate
for each 2-week period, set up the survey periods as strata and select
the option to
compute a separate estimate for each stratum.  You can still pool across
strata to estimate detection probability if needed or you can use covariates
that may change detection probability within and across strata.

regards--jeff

messages.subject: A simple density correction for changed survey effort?
messages.subject_clean: A simple density correction for changed survey effort?
messages.body_plain:
I analyzed point count data to estimate density of a number of bird species
- no problems there.  I miscalculated the survey effort as 50 when it
should have 60.  Other than re-running the analysis, is there an easy way
to correct the DISTANCE density estimates, e.g., using a simple percentage
correction?

messages.subject: sample size estimation
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance Samplers:

As part of an effort to monitor birds in a network of parks and
Monuments in Arizona, we are assessing sample size requirements for
estimating density at several levels of precision.  Because many of
our parks are small, obtaining enough samples to estimate density
within some parks is challenging.

As a planning exercise, we used the equations of Buckland et al.
2001, pgs 240-246 to determine the number of count stations and
visits required to annually estimate density with CV's ranging from
10 to 20% for species with varying encounter rates using pilot
data.  Due to low encounter rates for many species and a limited
number of stations that can be placed in small parks, estimating
density within some parks puts us over budget, even using relatively
high CV.  Although the problem could be remedied somewhat by repeated
sampling of the same stations, we hope to limit this effort to 4
cts/pt/yr so as to obtain greater spatial replication in larger
parks.  Pooling encounters and estimating among-park density, of
course, produces much more reasonable estimates of sample size, but
fails to provide information at the park level.

By pooling data across the network and considering parks as strata,
we assume estimating density by park could be improved.   Equations
for calculating sample size for stratified designs seem very complex
and are presented only in the context of line transects (see Buckland
et al. 2001, pgs 246-248).  First, how would we modify these
equations to estimate sample sizes for pt cts?  Second, will
stratification enable gains in efficiency if detectability is
relatively constant among strata and most of the same species occur
throughout the network?  And third, would an appropriate approach be
to use simulations to estimate sampling sizes across a range of CVs
using encounters from pilot data?  Our data could be resampled at
random to extend them beyond the ~20,000 encounters we have and the
behavior of estimates assessed across a range of sample sizes.

Any insights would surely be appreciated.

Aaron Flesch
Univ. of Arizona

--

messages.subject: Survey Design
messages.body_plain:
Hello

=20

Inspired by the paper by Thomas et al. (available at =
http://www.iwcoffice.org/_documents/sci_com/SC58docs/SC-58-IA16.pdf, and =
I highly recommend anyone interested in survey design to read this =
paper) I am trying to acquaint myself with the survey design module of =
DISTANCE. After having played around with the MEXICO sample project for =
a while, I have been trying to import my own shapes into DISTANCE. This =
has not proven to be an easy matter!

=20

I am not using ARC, but a program that supposedly exports shp files. =
After going through the recommended steps to import the files into =
DISTANCE, I found that my shapes looked odd, and the distances for =
output surveys did not make sense. I must be doing something simple =
wrong here but I can't figure out what it is.

=20

I then tried a simple experiment:

1. Opened a new project.

2. Input the following vertices for the polygon:        X         Y

                                                                        =
-10        60

                                                                        =
-10        61

                                                                        =
-9         61

                                                                        =
-9         60

My expectation is that this square should be 60 nm N to S and roughly 30 =
nm E to W.

=20

3. I set the project properties to WGS 1984, no projection, nautical =
mile units. I set the map properties to Albers projection with nautical =
mile units.

=20

4.	I then generated a coverage grid with one nm separation between =
points. This gave about the expected number of points (ca 1800).
5.	I then mapped the block and the coverage grid. It is 60 points E to W =
and about 30 N to S, exactly opposite my expectation.

=20

It appears that the shape has transposed lat-longs, but I can't figure =
out what is going on here. This happens with most of my export files as =
well.

=20

I would be interested to know if anyone is having similar problems =
getting geo data into DISTANCE, or if anyone has found a procedure that =
works consistently.

=20

Many thanks.

=20

Daniel Pike

Scientific Secretary

North Atlantic Marine Mammal Commission

Polar Environmental Centre

N-9296 Troms=F8, Norway

Tel.: +47 77 75 01 77

Fax: +47 77 75 01 81

danie...@nammco.no

=20

See us on the Web at www.nammco.no <http://www.nammco.no>.

=20

--
